The tres is a chordophone from Cuba, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.322-5. The commonest Cuban tres has six strings in three courses of two, and a body smaller than the Spanish guitar. Playing centres on the guajeo, an ostinato common in Afro-Cuban music, above all the Cuban son and changüí. The Puerto Rican version has nine strings and a body close to the Puerto Rican cuatro (cuatro).
Tres常見於古巴頌樂與非裔古巴音樂，也用於關塔那摩一帶的查恩吉、嫩貢、基里巴等: The tres is common in the Cuban son and in Afro-Cuban music, and is also used in the nineteenth-century styles around Guantánamo such as changüí, nengón and kiribá. Its playing centres on the guajeo ostinato, which can carry both rhythm and melody. In the United States it entered salsa line-ups and appears on Fania recordings; traditional Cuban playing can be heard on the recordings of the Guantánamo changüí group and of the Oviedo father and son.
Tres於十九世紀下半葉在古巴東部關塔那摩地區成形，最初用於昌古伊等音樂，並成為: The tres took shape in the second half of the nineteenth century in the Guantánamo area of eastern Cuba, was first used for music such as changüí, and became an important voice of the Cuban son. Its exact origin is unknown, and it is related in its development to the Spanish guitar, the laud and the bandurria. In the 1920s the popularity of the Cuban son spread the tres widely; in the 1930s several well-known players appeared, and a nine-string Puerto Rican version with a body close to the cuatro arose, possibly connected with Isaac Oviedo's visit to Puerto Rico in 1929. From the 1950s the tres was recorded electrically, and in the 1970s it appeared in salsa line-ups in the United States.

三弦古巴吉他的琴身通常採用檀木或雪松等優質共鳴木材製作，提供溫暖的諧波共鳴。琴頸: The body of the tres is usually of good resonant woods such as rosewood or cedar, which give warm harmonic resonance. The neck is mostly carved from Honduras mahogany or another hard wood, for stability. The pegs are of wood or light metal, and the strings of nylon or steel, usually in three pairs. The lining inside the body is of softwoods such as spruce, which improves the resonance.
三弦古巴吉他音色明亮清脆，具有獨特的穿透力，能在樂隊中清晰突出。其音域偏高，主要: The tres's timbre is bright and crisp, with a distinctive penetration that makes it stand out clearly in a band. Its range is high, mostly in the upper middle, and its timbre has a metallic quality and plenty of rhythm. It works by amplification through the resonator, whose internal cavity produces a warm harmonic resonance that rounds the sound. Beside a standard six-string guitar the tres is sharper and brighter, with the warm underpinning of Cuban local character; beside the mandolin it is deeper and fuller, better suited to rhythmic accompaniment. The instrument particularly suits traditional Cuban music, and its distinctive sound has added a signature colour to the music of Jamaica and the Caribbean.
